groups.text: A classic blocking server gives every connection its own thread.
Each thread calls read and waits for bytes.
Most connections are idle.
A point-of-sale terminal sends one request every ten seconds.
So almost every thread sits parked in read, doing nothing.
Each one still holds its own stack, about a megabyte of native memory.
Bytes arrive on one socket.
The kernel wakes that one thread, and the rest keep waiting.
Ten thousand connections need ten thousand threads, and almost all of them are waiting.
A Selector turns this around.
Put every channel in non-blocking mode, and register it with one selector.
Each registration is a SelectionKey.
It holds the interest set, the operations you care about, and the ready set, which the selector fills in.
Its attachment keeps that connection's state.
Now one thread runs a loop.
It calls select, which sleeps until at least one channel is ready.
On Linux, that is E poll underneath.
Two clients send data.
Their keys become ready, and select returns them in the selected-key set.
The thread serves only those two.
It reads what arrived, writes the reply, and moves on.
The four idle channels cost it nothing.
It must remove each handled key from the set itself.
The selector adds keys and never takes them out.
Leave one in, and the next pass handles it again with its old ready set.
Then it calls select again, and sleeps until the next channel is ready.
Here is that loop in Java and in Kotlin.
Select, walk the selected keys, remove each one, serve it.
A selector's selected-key set is not safe for several threads at once.
So one thread owns the selector and does all the work for its channels.
Netty calls that thread an event loop.
